  • Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it.
  • Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.

Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the latest version when you’re ready.

Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.

Sources indicate that retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request.

It has been revealed that tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences:.

It has been revealed that the persona, answerFormat, and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true, which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions. Table 1 reveals how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region.

Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction.

Recent findings suggest that these patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and company values, and persona and answerPolicy give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in answerPolicy and a set citation form in answerFormat, so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an answerFormat, without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller.

An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages:.

Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve.

Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls AgenticRetrieveStream on one shared managed knowledge base.

Figure 1: One managed knowledge base with per-tenant instructions and filters.

The same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.

According to recent reports, the example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has region, audience_team, and sensitivity metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them.

The code is in the GitHub repo, in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set AWS_REGION. For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions.

Examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines.

The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording:.

To create and pin each tenant’s instruction:.

According to recent reports, this code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5.

According to recent reports, an upgrade replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set customerEncryptionKeyArn when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions.

It has been revealed that an instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches.

Figure 2: Where tenant isolation comes from.

According to recent reports, A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter.

Industry observers note that with a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value.

Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends:.

In a recent development, this filter uses the equals, andAll, and orAll operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through userContext.

According to recent reports, answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter.

Sources indicate that for each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line. A tenant line is a short sentence, such as Customer sales region: Sales Region Central., placed before the question:.

Here’s the same return question answered with three tenant instructions on one knowledge base, trimmed:.

Industry observers note that A tenant line tells the agent who is asking, which helps the answer quote that tenant’s values. It doesn’t set the tenant’s language, answer format, or date and money formats, so pair it with the tenant’s instruction. Without the instruction, a Sales Region Central answer can come back in English, without the Source: line, or in the wrong date format.

It has been revealed that without an instruction, a customer answer can also quote internal discount tiers from a document the tenant can retrieve. An answer policy that forbids them, like the Sales Region Central one, can keep them out, but to make sure, filter out the document that contains them. Team formats such as the ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer, so validate the format in any code that depends on it.

In a recent development, instructions change how an answer is written. The facts still come from the documents the agent retrieves, so compute exact values such as a return deadline in your application.

Recent findings suggest that A request can reference only one retrieval instruction. When a user belongs to both a region and a team, that instruction has to cover both. For example, a support agent in Sales Region South needs the support team’s voice and the region’s date and money formats. Table 2 compares two ways to set that up for N regions and M teams.

Table 2: Two ways to cover a region and a team with one instruction.

According to recent reports, start with the team’s instruction and a region tenant line, which keeps the count at N + M. Add a combined instruction only for pairs whose formats differ from the team’s default. Neither approach limits what the agent retrieves, so keep the tenant filter on every request. A filter also can’t remove a value from a shared document the tenant is entitled to, such as a global policy that lists every region’s dates. As of this writing, the default quota is 50 retrieval instructions per account per AWS Region, and you can request an increase. Combined instructions add up promptly, with 15 for 3 regions and 3 teams and 65 for 10 regions and 5 teams.

According to recent reports, if your application calls agentic retrieval with the same role for every tenant, IAM can’t tell tenants apart, and your code alone chooses each request’s instruction and filter. When each tenant’s requests run under that tenant’s own credentials, tag conditions add a second check on which instruction a request can apply and who can change it. Those credentials can come from a role per tenant or a role assumed with a tenant session tag.

Recent findings suggest that agenticRetrieveStream has no IAM resource. To apply an instruction, the caller needs bedrock:GetRetrievalInstruction on the instruction’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so that’s where the tag condition goes. These attribute-based access control (ABAC) statements from the example’s AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app scope one tenant:.

With these statements, a tenant’s applier role can apply only instructions tagged with its tenant, and its tenant admin role can manage only those instructions. The platform admin can manage any tenant’s instructions. Require both tag conditions on TagResource. With only the request-tag condition, a tenant admin can retag another tenant’s instruction into its own scope. To add a tenant, add its key to the tenantRoles context value and deploy the AWS CDK app again with the same trustedPrincipalArn. Apply permission doesn’t limit retrieval, so scope bedrock:Retrieve to each role’s knowledge bases. ListRetrievalInstructions can’t be scoped by tag, so keep instruction names free of sensitive information.

As Use retrieval instructions with agentic retrieval describes, the first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction, with the ID and version of the instruction that was applied. Log it with the tenant ID:.

Recent findings suggest that for every event type, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference. To capture the applied instruction, check for the first Planning event in the loop that reads the answer:.

According to recent reports, for an audit record outside your application, use AWS CloudTrail. CloudTrail logs Agents for Amazon Bedrock Runtime operations, including AgenticRetrieveStream, as data events. A trail records data events only after you enable them. For details, see Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail.

In a recent development, amazon Bedrock doesn’t route traffic between versions. Keep a release configuration for each tenant, pin its version on every request, and canary, promote, or roll back by changing that pin. The trace confirms which version served each request, not whether the new version answers better, so gate each promotion on your own checks. This release configuration is from the repo’s router:.

To change one tenant, patch its instruction, wait for the review, create a version, and move only that tenant’s pin. For example, moving the support tenant to version 2 leaves the other five tenants on version 1:.

Industry observers note that A pin fixes the instruction, not the exact wording of each answer. During an revision review, DRAFT keeps serving the previous content. A version create or a second update during the review fails with HTTP 409, so poll until the review finishes, as the retrieval instruction rollout steps describe.

Retrieval instructions aren’t only for multi-tenant setups. The same fields work for a single application, such as an assistant that has to return JSON for downstream code or keep one voice across every answer. The repo has code for the first three.

An answerFormat can replace your own generation step:.

With this answerFormat, agentic retrieval can return the JSON directly, so you don’t need a separate generation step. Validate the JSON in your code before you use it.

Give each audience its own persona and answerFormat, such as a customer answer and a ticket note, so the same knowledge bases can serve them all without mixing their formats.

Several retrievers can share one instruction version:.

Recent findings suggest that set identity, tone, and language once in persona, such as “Use a friendly, concise tone. Reply in the language of the question.”.

Put required lines in answerPolicy and citation forms in answerFormat, and give a realistic citation example, such as Source: central-returns-addendum.md, instead of a placeholder.

Use answerPolicy to name the fallback, such as “If the documents do not answer the question, say so and give the support contact.”.

Use retrievalGuidance for acronyms and preferred sources, such as “Treat model numbers as exact-match terms.” Check the Planning trace events to see how the agent searched. Use filters, not guidance, to limit what it retrieves.

Follow these practices when you write and roll out retrieval instructions:.

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the retrieval instructions with the following commands. Then follow the cleanup steps in the repo README for the knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and roles.

Retrieval instructions give each tenant its own voice, answer format, date and money formats, and answer policy on shared managed knowledge bases. Pair them with metadata filters to keep tenant data apart and pinned versions to roll out changes one tenant at a time. The trace indicates which version answered, and CloudTrail can record the AgenticRetrieveStream calls. Tag conditions add a check when tenants have their own credentials.

In a recent development, to get started, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference and the GitHub repo. To learn more, read Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.

Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, with Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword.
  • When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:.
  • Industry observers note that the rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended.

When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:.

Industry observers note that the rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t.

Recent findings suggest that to ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things.

Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope.

Must-block list (from legal and compliance):.

Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do):.

Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them currently blocking legitimate queries:.

Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight sections work through the practices, most of them closing with a “Back at AnyCompany Bank” subsection that highlights the fix applied to this scenario. The post then closes with the one limitation to plan for regardless of how well you follow the practices: results are not fully deterministic.

According to recent reports, note: Denied Topic structure in Standard tier. A topic has three parts, a name, a definition, and up to five examples, and the guardrail evaluates all three together as a single unit, not the definition alone. The name can be up to 100 characters. The definition can be up to 1,000 characters, with 100–300 as the practical sweet spot. Each example can be up to 100 characters, and a guardrail can hold up to 30 topics.

Recent findings suggest that this practice sets the general frame. Best practices 2 through 4 apply it to each part of a topic in turn: the name, the definition, and the examples.

Industry observers note that A frequent reason a topic blocks legitimate queries is that the topic describes a subject domain rather than what the user wants from the exchange. Two queries in the same domain can carry different intentions. “When does my direct deposit clear?” and “How much does an L5 engineer earn?” both concern pay, but only the second is a salary comparison. A domain-framed topic collapses those distinctions and can block queries semantically near the domain. A topic framed around the user’s intention matches only queries where that intention is present.

Sources indicate that intention is the framing lens. To make it operational, name the topic after the specific action or content type that expresses the intention on the surface, such as a request, a claim, or a piece of generated content. Intention tells you what to catch, and action gives you a concrete shape the guardrail can evaluate.

It has been revealed that the guardrail evaluates both the topic name and its definition together. When either component names a domain, the topic matches too broadly. When both name an action that expresses a specific intention, the topic is precise.

Recent findings suggest that the next few best practices apply this idea to AnyCompany Bank’s own topics, with concrete examples. Best practice 2 renames them, and Best practice 3 tightens their definitions to match.

The topic name has a meaningful effect on what is matched, often greater than expected. A broad category name (Finance, Security, Legal) can lead the guardrail to associate the topic with vocabulary in that category, even when the definition attempts to narrow the scope. A specific action name (Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, Suing for Damages) helps narrow the scope before the definition is read.

One of AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topics was named Legal:.

Recent findings suggest that this is why “Can you help me modify my mortgage?” got blocked. Mortgages are legal instruments, so queries about them live in the semantic neighborhood of legal. Renaming solves half the problem before we even touch the definition:.

The new name uses a verb-derived noun (litigation), names a second specific behavior (non-servicing legal advice), and makes clear by contrast that servicing questions, such as modifications, forbearance, and escrow, are outside the topic. The name itself now carries some of the work the definition would otherwise do alone.

Recent findings suggest that anyCompany Bank applied the same logic to the Fraud topic, renaming it to Fraud Investigation Requests. The assistant should still let customers report fraud, which gets routed to a human, but must not attempt to investigate fraud claims itself.

After these three renames, AnyCompany Bank’s topic list is:.

The definition should describe the user’s action on a specific object, rather than the general subject of that action.

We recommend the following structure:[Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].

AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic was named Finance, with a definition to match:.

In a recent development, this is exactly why “Where can I find my payoff quote?” was blocked. Payoff is a financial term, quote concerns money, and the input is “related to” the finance domain, even though the customer’s intention, retrieving a servicing figure, has nothing to do with what AnyCompany Bank wanted to refuse.

Following Best practice 1, the team renamed the topic to Investment Recommendations and adjusted the definition’s vocabulary to match, without yet making it action-scoped:.

Recent findings suggest that this was still domain-framed even though the name had improved. General education (“Explain what a mutual fund is”), historical financial news (“Why did rates rise last quarter?”), and portfolio review (“Show me my holdings”) all matched. The assistant should answer all of them.

The team applied the structural template, with an action opener, specific objects, a qualifying constraint, and one or two sub-cases:.

Industry observers note that every piece of the template serves a specific purpose. “Asking for a personalized recommendation to…” is the action opener. “Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” are the specific objects. “For the user’s own investment returns” is the qualifying constraint that excludes educational and third-party discussion. The “Includes…” clause names two sub-cases: a specific-security question and an allocation-percentage question.

AnyCompany Bank applied the same template to the Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests topics:.

The team now had three named topics with action-scoped definitions.

Examples teach the guardrail where the boundaries of your topic are. Not every example does this equally well. Five paraphrases of the same idea teach the guardrail nothing fresh, while five carefully chosen examples can draw the outline of the topic with much less definition text. The examples that carry the most weight are the ones sitting near the topic’s edge, close enough to a plausible non-match that they show the guardrail where to draw the line. We call these boundary examples. A good boundary example has three properties. First, it’s inside the topic’s scope. Second, it’s close to a plausible non-match, using vocabulary or structure that resembles inputs the topic should not match. Third, it differs from your other examples in sub-case, sentence shape, and vocabulary.

The team’s first pass at examples for Investment Recommendations looked like this:.

These are five ways of asking the same question. During testing, the assistant blocked “Should I buy stocks?” reliably. But it let through “Is it a good time to rotate my portfolio out of equities into bonds?”, which is exactly the kind of question the topic is supposed to catch. The paraphrases had crowded around one point in the topic, and other points were unguarded.

The rewrite spread the examples across sub-cases and sentence shapes:.

Industry observers note that these are five different sub-cases (specific stock, asset-class shift, allocation, sell timing, growth screen) and five different sentence shapes, all inside the topic. Adjacent non-matches like “Explain what an ETF is” (educational) and “Show me my portfolio report” (data retrieval) are sufficiently different from the examples that the guardrail should not match them.

Recent findings suggest that the team applied the same treatment to Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests. The original Litigation examples were all variants of “Can I sue?” The rewritten set covered lawsuit filing, formal legal opinions, class-action inquiries, damages, and rights-interpretation. The original Fraud Investigation Requests examples were all variants of “Someone stole my money, what do I do?” The rewritten set covered unauthorized-charge investigation, card-fraud tracing, transaction reversal, identity-theft adjudication, and scammer tracing. Each rewritten set covers five different sub-cases inside one topic.

At this point, AnyCompany Bank’s three topics pass every test written so far. One more problem only reveals up after the assistant runs against real traffic.

Some concepts are inherently ambiguous, because the same words describe both a matching and non-matching action, depending on context. In these cases, add an explicit anchor that fixes the context: an institutional setting, a stated purpose, or a dual condition of the form “only applies when both X and Y are present”.

In a recent development, adding an insider-trading topic exposed the ambiguity matter. The compliance team wanted Insider Trading Advice as a distinct topic, narrower and more serious than the general Investment Recommendations catch. The first draft:.

This matched the expected case: a customer asking for a trade based on private information. It also matched something the team didn’t expect: educational queries about what insider trading is, phrased as questions. “How does the SEC define insider trading?” was getting blocked, because it “asks about insider trading”.

According to recent reports, both conditions should rule out educational queries: they fail condition 2, because they don’t describe non-public information the user personally holds. When the team tested “How does the SEC define insider trading?” against this definition, it still got blocked some of the time. The anchor was not the problem. The topic’s name was: it repeats the exact phrase the query uses. The guardrail weighs the name as a signal independent of the definition, the same effect Best practice 2 describes elsewhere. A dual-condition anchor can specify the right conditions and still lose to a name built from the term that it’s trying to disambiguate.

The team kept the anchor and renamed the topic instead:.

With the rename, the educational query passed reliably, and the real examples, the ones naming a specific security and a specific piece of non-public information, still blocked.

In a recent development, the definition is longer than the 100–300 character target from Best practice 3, and that is deliberate. The ambiguity here justifies the extra text. The topic itself is inherently subtle, so the definition has to carry more work.

In a recent development, A guardrail evaluates its topics together, not one at a time. When two topics have similar meanings, they interfere with each other. It becomes difficult to predict which topic the guardrail reports as the match, and the combined effect can block legitimate inputs that neither topic alone would block. Overlap between topics is often the reason a well-written topic produces incorrect results. The problem isn’t that topic, but a neighboring topic.

Recent findings suggest that suppose, late in the process, AnyCompany Bank’s compliance team proposed adding a broader Financial Advice topic alongside the already-defined Investment Recommendations. The intuition was that the broader topic would catch requests the specific one missed. Both topics were drafted with their own definitions:.

Sources indicate that the overlap became visible when the team tested “Should I put more into my 401(k)?”. Depending on how the caller ordered the topics in the API request, either Topic A, Topic B, or both would report the match, and on some orderings the guardrail blocked the input.

Industry observers note that anyCompany Bank consolidated. Financial Advice was removed, and Investment Recommendations was left to carry the specific action. After the consolidation, the ordering-dependent variance disappeared. The same input produced the same verdict regardless of where topics sat in the API call, which is the primary win from removing the overlap.

The 401(k) query itself, however, was not fully resolved by consolidation alone. Because “Should I put more into my 401(k)?” shares its “Should I put more…” frame with a real trading recommendation, Investment Recommendations still matches it on the surface. This is a residual boundary case that consolidation can’t fix by itself. It’s exactly the kind of structurally-similar match that Best practice 8 warns a trailing exclusion can’t reliably override.

Sources indicate that the team also reordered the remaining topics. The original order was:.

Sources indicate that topics 1 and 2 both discuss securities and cover related financial actions, so adjacent placement invited attribution ambiguity for borderline inputs. The team interleaved them:.

Recent findings suggest that litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice now sits between the two securities-adjacent topics. Borderline questions like “Should I trade my Example Corp shares based on rumor?” now attribute more consistently to Trading on Non-Public Information rather than flipping between Trading on Non-Public Information and Investment Recommendations.

Denied Topics is the right tool when the rule you need to enforce is specific to your business and expressible as a short description of the content. Think of a regulatory line, a policy commitment, a legal risk, or a scope boundary, rather than a universal safety category or a fixed list of words. Guardrails offers several policies that share the same goal of blocking specific content, but each is designed for a different kind of signal. Using Denied Topics for a category that another policy handles natively tends to block too much or too little, complicates your configuration, and produces worse results. A carefully written topic for a category that Content Filter already covers is usually less effective than Content Filter for that category.

Note that enabling more than one policy in the same guardrail incurs additional cost, because each enabled policy is evaluated on every request. When you compose Denied Topics with Content Filter or Prompt Attack, plan for the combined cost.

Industry observers note that looking back at AnyCompany Bank’s must-block list (from the scenario at the start of the post), three of the six items are not really Denied Topics at all. They belong to policies that Guardrails already provides natively.

After this cleanup, AnyCompany Bank’s guardrail configuration composes multiple policies:.

Denied Topics carries only the four bank-specific rules that no other policy can express.

The following patterns cause topics to block the wrong inputs even when the rest of the definition is otherwise well written. Avoid them. Most are a specific case of guidance already given in earlier best practices, so each line that follows points back to where the full reasoning lives.

A short trailing exclusion isn’t a general-purpose fix for every false refusal. It reliably rules out queries that are categorically different from the topic, such as a different intent, a different asker, or a different type of content. It’s less reliable when a benign query is worded almost exactly like the definition’s positive language, only about a different object. In that case, the exclusion competes against wording it closely resembles, and the match often wins.

For that structurally-similar case, prefer one of these three alternatives instead:.

Recent findings suggest that A trailing exclusion remains the right first move for every other case. Reach for one of these three only when testing shows the exclusion is losing to a near-identical match.

In a recent development, even a guardrail that follows every practice in this post won’t produce fully deterministic results across every possible input. Denied Topics reads meaning with a language model, and language-model evaluations carry some inherent variance. There are two forms of this variance you should plan for.

Recent findings suggest that variance when repeating the exact same request. Sending the identical input to the identical guardrail configuration two times in a row can, in rare cases, produce different results. The same characters go in, the same topic list applies, everything is the same, and yet one call blocks and the next passes. For most inputs, and for topics that follow the preceding guidance, this doesn’t happen, and the result is stable across repeated calls. The exceptions are borderline inputs, whose meaning sits close to the semantic edge of a topic. Those are the ones prone to flipping on repeat. The more precisely a topic is defined (action-scoped, specific objects, clear anchor, boundary examples), the fewer of your inputs fall in that borderline zone.

Variance when the topic list changes. The guardrail evaluates all topics together with the input on every request. Changes to the topic list, such as adding a topic, removing one, or reordering the same topics, can shift results for previously-tested inputs. An input that was blocked with one topic list might pass with a different one. This effect happens more when two topics share meaning or when a topic definition is broad. It happens less when every topic in the list has a specific, action-scoped definition and clear boundary examples. Applying the practices in this post meaningfully reduces both forms of variance.

Note: Every pass-or-fail claim in this post was tested end-to-end against Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (Standard tier), each query repeated multiple times to confirm the result was stable.

To recap, the practices in this post come down to eight points:.

Denied Topics is a powerful policy. With it, you can describe a bespoke content category in a short natural-language definition, without training a classifier or hand-crafting regular expressions. That power depends on describing the category the way the guardrail reads it: as the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action on a specific object, not as a subject domain. Get the framing right and the rest of the practices in this post, such as naming, definition, examples, anchors, overlap management, and policy selection, fall into place naturally.

Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval.
  • A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer.
  • Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps.

A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook.

Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read.

In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read.

According to recent reports, retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape:.

It has been revealed that retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy.

In a recent development, tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps.

Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?”.

Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search.

In agentic retrieval, an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on.

When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages:.

Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values.

Sources indicate that an AgenticRetrieveStream request can search one knowledge base or several. The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code.

Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others.

Recent findings suggest that tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema.

In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines calculations over your tables with facts from your documents. It cites the passages it used, and the trace names the table files the code read.

According to recent reports, in Figure 1, an Amazon S3 data source syncs these files into the knowledge base, which keeps embeddings, text, metadata, and the original files. When your application sends a question with AgenticRetrieveStream, agentic retrieval plans the work and retrieves passages from the knowledge base. If the question needs data from a table file, it sends the files to read to an isolated sandbox with no network access. There, model-written code runs over the original file and returns printed results. The answer, with citations and trace events, streams back to your application.

Figure 1: Table files and documents in an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, with tabular search inside agentic retrieval.

Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries.
  • Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges.
  • Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization.

Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility.

Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how swiftly life-saving medicines reach patients.

To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes.

We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible.

Recent findings suggest that teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once:.

In a recent development, conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing.

It has been revealed that the assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern.

In a recent development, the reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda. The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK).

At a high level, a question flows through the system like this:.

According to recent reports, figure 1: End-to-end architecture where a query agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore uses Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, embeddings, and reranking, with hybrid retrieval across Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon Neptune linked by shared document numbers. An event-driven, serverless ingestion pipeline populates both stores, while memory, observability, and evaluations support personalization, monitoring, and quality assessment.

The graph is organized around two complementary layers, which is what lets the assistant take into account where a document sits and what it is about.

High-level taxonomy: The process tree. The organization’s official process framework is modeled as a hierarchy of process nodes (roughly three levels, parent to child). Each controlled document is attached to the lowest applicable process level, so each onboarded document has a known place. This lets the assistant scope a question to a process area before retrieving anything, and automatically categorize newly ingested documents.

Recent findings suggest that low-level taxonomy: Domain entities. SMEs define the entities that make an answer correct or incorrect in manufacturing: sites, product generations, equipment, process steps, and similar attributes. These are modeled as first-class graph nodes linked to the documents that describe them, using a small set of unified relationship types rather than an ever-growing list of edge names.

Modeling both layers is what distinguishes a genuine GraphRAG system from two databases side by side. The document number on an OpenSearch passage is also a node in the graph, so a search hit is an immediate entry point into the graph’s structure with no fuzzy re-matching required. This chunk-to-graph bridge is a key design choice in the retrieval path.

In a recent development, early GraphRAG work favored open-ended extraction, letting a language model discover entities with no fixed schema. This approach is powerful for open-ended sensemaking over sprawling text, but it is noisy, hard to maintain, and difficult to audit. Over the past couple of years, the consensus has shifted toward ontology-guided extraction using a predefined, domain-specific schema to guide the model, which improves accuracy and reliability for specialized corpora.

Sources indicate that for regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing this is not a compromise, but the right default. The domain already has a real ontology, curated by experts, and a fixed schema with a human-in-the-loop promotion process for new entities supports the auditability the team needed in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The design aligns with where much of the field has moved since early open-schema approaches, while making design decisions easier to explain to quality and audit stakeholders.

Each store covers the other’s blind spot:.

Recent findings suggest that A common pattern is vector finds the seeds, the graph expands from them, and the reverse for relationship-first questions. A reranking stage (a cross-encoder through Amazon Bedrock Rerank) sits after fusion: it reads the question and each candidate passage together and reorders them, adding a precision pass on top of the cheaper recall stage before anything reaches the model.

A distinctive part of the assistant is how it handles ambiguity. A question like “which samples are taken on the granulator?” has several correct answers depending on product generation, site, equipment, and batch size. Answering immediately risks a confident, wrong, out-of-scope response, which is the worst outcome in a regulated setting.

Guided mode inverts the usual RAG order: instead of retrieving first, the agent narrows scope through clarification first, then searches. This follows recent research on clarifying ambiguous questions before retrieval and on using a knowledge graph to supply the clarification options rather than letting the model invent them. It uses two classes of scope:.

This keeps clarification options grounded in real data (designed to help reduce the risk of hallucinated options) and it scales: when experts add a latest distinguishing attribute to the taxonomy, the assistant surfaces it automatically, without requiring changes to prompts or code.

Accuracy here is defined narrowly and enforced deliberately:.

An automated evaluation harness checks responses against these criteria: relevant-source selection, valid document status, latest applicable version, scope compliance, citation accuracy, and faithful preservation of requirement strength (must, should, or may) so behavior can be measured as the system evolves.

It has been revealed that the wider vault this solution sits on top of holds on the order of four million documents. At that scale, the problem is not a shortage of information but the near-impossibility of finding the exactly right, in-scope, current answer by hand. Traditional enterprise search returns long lists ranked by keyword overlap and leaves the hard work to the person asking. This includes deciding which result applies, which version is effective, and how documents relate.

This solution turns the vault into an intelligent, answer-first search engine, and the two-layer taxonomy is what makes that tractable at scale:.

The design is intended to scale with the vault rather than degrade as it grows: the larger and more interconnected the documentation, the more value the graph and scoping add.

According to recent reports, depending on the type of task an SME is doing (searching for an answer, updating a document, or adapting one for a new context), work that used to take hours or days is reduced to minutes. Beyond raw time saved, the solution changes what is practical to do at all:.

Just as important in a regulated setting, the assistant’s design to clarify scope and flag missing or ambiguous content helps reduce the risk of confident, out-of-scope answers, where the real cost of a mistake lies.

Industry observers note that the Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area collaborated with AWS to build this solution, with subject-matter experts and data and AI engineers working closely throughout. The taxonomy that makes the assistant accurate comes directly from the group’s domain experts. The retrieval and agent architecture was designed and iterated with AWS.

In a recent development, building a prototype was key to getting the solution to go live. Rather than debating capabilities in the abstract, the team put a working system in front of subject-matter experts early. They tested it against real questions and used what they learned to sharpen the taxonomy, the retrieval path, and the guided-mode behavior. The prototype turned an ambitious idea into something people could try, critique, and trust. It also de-risked the architecture decisions before any broader rollout.

By combining a curated knowledge graph, hybrid search, and a clarify-before-retrieve agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area built a process-intelligence assistant that is fast where speed helps and grounded where accuracy matters. The design applies current GraphRAG patterns to regulated manufacturing: ontology-guided extraction, a bridged two-store retrieval path, graph-grounded disambiguation, and reranking. This turns a large documentation landscape into grounded, cited answers with room to extend to new domains.

Industry observers note that to get started building your own agentic AI solution, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for managed agent runtime, tool orchestration, and observability at scale. The agent runtimes in this post were built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source, framework agnostic toolkit you can use with your own retrieval stack. For GraphRAG reference architectures using Amazon Neptune and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, visit the AWS Architecture Center.

Tech Report: Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire.
  • According to recent reports, this post indicates you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock, Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints.
  • Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire. We have seen this situation again and again while working with banking, insurance, and airline customers. Their Assembler programs still run critical business operations, but fewer people can read them each year. Rewriting them by hand takes years, risks breaking business rules nobody remembers writing, and still depends on the same experts who are leaving. Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform change that equation.

According to recent reports, this post indicates you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock, Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints. You will learn how to systematically extract business rules from Assembler code, convert them through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized applications as Java Spring Boot services on AWS.

Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have:.

It has been revealed that you can transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications tightly bounded with COBOL into Java Spring Boot applications built for the AWS cloud through a systematic five-phase approach. This multi-stage methodology, converting Assembler to COBOL as an intermediate step before Java transformation, reduces risk and preserves business logic with greater reliability than direct Assembler-to-Java conversion. The intermediate COBOL stage provides a structured, human-readable format that subject matter experts (SMEs) can validate before final transformation. This makes sure that business rules remain intact throughout the modernization journey. The following sections describe both the current mainframe architecture and the target cloud-focused state.

Your current architecture represents a traditional mainframe environment where Assembler programs execute batch processes, connected with COBOL, interact with databases, and process files. At its core, JCL (Job Control Language) jobs trigger Assembler program execution at scheduled intervals. These programs read input from VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) and sequential files and perform operations against IBM Db2 for z/OS. Your business logic executes using low-level register operations (direct CPU register manipulation) and memory management. Output is written back to files or database tables, and job completion status is reported through JCL return codes. All of this runs on IBM z/OS mainframe infrastructure.

Figure 1: Mainframe Assembler architecture.

The modernization solution helps you transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the AWS cloud through a multi-phase, AI-powered workflow. The architecture uses Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for AI-assisted code analysis and business rule extraction, and AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion.

If COBOL source code is already available, you follow the conventional approach and provide it directly to AWS Transform for conversion to Java Spring Boot applications.

You begin the transformation workflow by analyzing Assembler code to generate Business Rules Extraction (BRE) documentation. In a recent development, the quality of your Business Rules Extraction (BRE) directly impacts transformation accuracy, so focus carefully on this phase. Use Amazon Bedrock, through Kiro IDE or the Amazon Bedrock console, along with AWS Transform for mainframe to extract and document business rules from your Assembler source code.

You can use the prompts in this post directly in Amazon Bedrock through the Chat Playground, or within Kiro IDE using its built-in AI chat and Spec panel. Replace the placeholder values with your actual Assembler code and context before running.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Bedrock is the inference platform behind the first four phases: business rules extraction, specification creation, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, and validation. Choose a foundation model with strong code reasoning and a large context window, because Assembler programs are long and dense. Set the temperature to 0 so you get consistent output across runs. To process many programs, call the same prompts through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and store each output in your Amazon S3 bucket so it can feed the next phase. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your prompts or model outputs to train AWS models or share them with third parties. For details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock. Use sanitized test data instead of production data or personally identifiable information (PII).

The more context you provide to the AI, the better it understands the business intent behind the code. Include relevant documentation, data dictionaries, and available business context alongside the Assembler code when prompting.

You should treat testing as an ongoing activity throughout the transformation process, not only a final phase. How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.
  • A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy.
  • The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.

A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions.

The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.

It has been revealed that this capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business owners and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead.

Industry observers note that moEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result.

MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.

Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.

Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work:.

Sources indicate that conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer.

Recent findings suggest that custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes.

According to recent reports, decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system.

It has been revealed that the architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others.

In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer.

The following diagram highlights how these components connect.

Figure 1: MoEngage Merlin AI architecture on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore runtime.

Sources indicate that moEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation.

The following simplified example highlights the pattern:.

The tools fall into five groups:.

Recent findings suggest that the tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions patch with it.

Recent findings suggest that A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state.

Sources indicate that on top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it.

Give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.

AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs.

Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session. Together, these capabilities let the team focus on agent logic and marketing intelligence rather than hosting infrastructure.

Inference through Amazon Bedrock gave MoEngage two more benefits. Merlin AI agents run on Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock, and MoEngage moves between these versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API. MoEngage also pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale.

The following example highlights how a user builds a campaign without leaving the conversation.

Draft a weekend flash sale push for our high-value segment, using the same tone as our best-performing December campaign.

Recent findings suggest that the agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. It returns a draft with several copy variants.

Which push notifications last month had below 2% click-through rate (CTR), and what do they have in common?

The Campaign Insights Agent compares those campaigns and reports the shared pattern, such as send time or audience overlap.

Show me the drop-off at step 3 of our onboarding flow, and pause the SMS branch if it’s below 5% conversion.

In a recent development, the agent reads the flow state through the flow tools and pauses the branch after the user confirms. This is the human-review mode in practice.

Each step uses the same tools that power the MoEngage interface. The user does not open a separate dashboard.

Merlin AI agents on this architecture have been in production for more than 6 months. One customer, Glance, reached campaign go-live 50% faster and saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates. With Merlin AI Copywriter, Glance teams also produce about three times more content variants per campaign.

Sources indicate that across the platform, MoEngage reports a 60–70% reduction in manual effort by marketing and product teams for channel, timing, and frequency decisions, and a 20–30% improvement in conversion rates from goal-based decisioning. Managed, pay-per-token inference in Amazon Bedrock reduced AI infrastructure costs by more than 50% compared with self-hosted models.

It has been revealed that agentCore feature availability varies by AWS Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

MoEngage made its platform agent-ready without rebuilding it. Existing OpenAPI specifications became MCP tools. AgentCore runtime provided hosting, authentication, and session isolation. Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock provided reasoning and generation. The result is a platform where marketing and product teams move from question to action in one conversation, where MoEngage engineers spend their time on marketing intelligence rather than infrastructure, and where agents handle workflows for the team and decisions for every customer while users stay in control.

The same pattern applies to other software providers with a mature API surface. Start from your existing specifications, keep identity outside the model, and let a managed runtime handle the production concerns.

Sources indicate that to build your own MCP server on the same foundation, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and follow the AgentCore runtime guide to host it. To choose a foundation model for your agents and review the security and data-handling controls, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To generate MCP tools from your existing OpenAPI specifications, review the FastMCP documentation. To see Merlin AI in action, visit MoEngage Merlin AI. To strategy a similar architecture, contact your AWS account team or Solutions Architect.
