How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that arisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology spanning pharmacovigilance, regulatory, medical affairs, clinical, and quality functions, developed NavaX, an AI engine purpose-built for life sciences on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing.
  • Industry observers note that arisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request.
  • ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that arisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology spanning pharmacovigilance, regulatory, medical affairs, clinical, and quality functions, developed NavaX, an AI engine purpose-built for life sciences on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching. As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months, while per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.

Industry observers note that arisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request. That left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth.

ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue (source: ArisGlobal press release). The entire system runs on AWS.

Sources indicate that lifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal’s AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. ArisGlobal productionized their first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic’s Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal’s internal production telemetry, they have processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments, handling billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. Model availability varies by Region. See Model support by AWS Region.

When a pharmaceutical organization receives an adverse-event report, typically a multipage PDF describing a patient’s reaction to a medication, NavaX’s Dynamic Data Extraction (DDE) agent extracts around 130 fields. These fields include patient demographics, suspect drugs, reporter information, event timelines, seriousness criteria, and regulatory classifications. Because this content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment. It draws on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter content and detect or mask sensitive information. Extracted fields are also validated against the schema and grounded in the source document.

In a recent development, this extraction happens across multiple sequential requests to the model. Each request focuses on a different section of the case form, and each carries:.

Industry observers note that two inputs repeat at different scopes. The shared prompt prefix includes the system rules, extraction schema, and few-shot examples. It repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent. The source document repeats only for the requests associated with one case.

According to recent reports, when NavaX rolled out with its first enterprise tenant, the system prompt was lean. As ArisGlobal onboarded additional pharmaceutical companies, each brought specific requirements:.

Sources indicate that over 6 months, the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens, a 150% increase. With multiple sequential requests per case, per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.

The prefix grew with every tenant and was reprocessed on every request, so prompt growth compounded with transaction volume.

Table 1 compares the original document-first request order with the production prompt-first design.

Amazon Bedrock prompt caching reduces latency and input token costs by caching a contiguous prompt prefix from the start of a request through a cache checkpoint. A later request with the same prefix can read cached tokens at a reduced rate instead of processing them again. Cache entries have a time-to-live (TTL) that resets after a successful cache hit.

Caching is prefix-based rather than block-based. Request sections are evaluated in sequence—tools, system, then messages—so changing an earlier section invalidates matching content that follows it.

Sources indicate that with explicit cache checkpoints, you can choose the exact prefix boundary. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request.

Industry observers note that with simplified cache management, you place one checkpoint after static content. Amazon Bedrock searches backward from that point for the longest matching prefix, up to about 20 content blocks.

Industry observers note that arisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request.

This reverses the initial request order. Because only a prefix can be cached, ordering determines which content can be reused.

The first design put the 10–200 page source document at the start of each request and placed the checkpoint after it. The shared prompt prefix and section-specific question followed the checkpoint.

The design reused the document within one case: the first request wrote it to cache, and later requests for that case read it at the reduced rate.

The next case used a different document and required a fresh cache write, so reuse never extended across cases or tenants.

It has been revealed that more importantly, the shared prompt prefix remained after the checkpoint and was processed at the full input rate on every request. The content driving the cost curve was excluded from the cache.

The production design changed the order rather than adding another checkpoint: the shared prompt prefix comes first, the checkpoint follows it, and the document comes last.

The same checkpoint now creates a reusable fleet-wide cache entry:.

ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet. The shared prefix is also the part that grows as customers are added.

According to recent reports, for most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently. This traffic keeps the shared prefix warm during business hours because each cache hit resets the TTL.

A second checkpoint after the document would cache a combined prefix consisting of the shared prompt and that case’s document. The entry would still be unique to one case.

ArisGlobal therefore prioritized the prefix whose reads amortize across the fleet. The shared prompt prefix scales across cases and tenants. The per-case document does not.

Recent findings suggest that in production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Figure 1 shows cache reads consistently exceeding cache writes.

It has been revealed that figure 1: Amazon CloudWatch prompt-cache usage. The blue cache-read series rises to roughly 10 times the cache-write series during periods of production traffic.

Caching the shared prompt prefix produced the following results while the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile remained in place:.

Industry observers note that figure 2: End-to-end invocation latency. The chart demonstrates a lower and more stable latency range after prompt-cache adoption.

According to recent reports, figure 3: Invocation count. The chart shows sustained production request volume while inference spend grew less than proportionally.

Based on ArisGlobal’s production billing data, serving 65% of input tokens from cache reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%. At more than 19 billion tokens per month, this produced approximately 40% overall monthly savings in inference spend.

Note: All performance and cost figures in this section reflect ArisGlobal’s production metrics as reported to AWS. Results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.

ArisGlobal’s experience offers guidance for many workloads with large, repeated prompt prefixes:.

Recent findings suggest that cache what repeats, not what is largest. A large per-case document offers limited reuse, while a byte-identical shared prompt prefix can serve requests across the fleet.

Put stable content first. Order tool definitions, system instructions, schemas, and examples before the checkpoint. Place tenant identifiers, case data, and the per-request question afterward.

It has been revealed that use fleet traffic to amortize cache writes. Requests from tenants using the same agent can read the same prefix, and cache hits reset the TTL. For sporadic traffic, evaluate the 1-hour TTL on supported models.

Reduce avoidable calls. Each call still processes the uncached document, so bundle sequential questions when output limits and schema requirements permit.

Industry observers note that keep the prefix byte-identical. Timestamps, request IDs, tenant names, and reordered tool definitions can cause misses. Move every dynamic element after the checkpoint.

Monitor the production baseline. Track cache reads, cache writes, and total input tokens in CloudWatch. Alert on a sustained drop below the normal 65% cache-hit baseline rather than using an incompatible 80% threshold.

Check model-specific limits. Prefix minimums and TTL options vary by model. Claude Sonnet 4.5 requires at least 1,024 tokens for a cache checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that arisGlobal combined EU geographic cross-Region inference with prompt caching aimed at the right content. Caching the stable shared prefix instead of the per-case document reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%, contributed to approximately 40% overall monthly inference savings, and supported around 15% more enterprise tenants without proportional cost increases.

Recent findings suggest that the key lesson is that cache value depends on reuse, not size. For multi-tenant agentic workloads, a repeated shared prompt prefix can be more valuable than a larger document that changes for every case.

To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation, the cross-Region inference guide, and the AWS blog post Effectively use prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock.

General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect an industrial control system network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Industrial control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. #1277. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Industry observers note that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Industry observers note that most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Sources indicate that getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

In a recent development, we declared Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

It has been revealed that phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the key things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Industry observers note that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

In a recent development, we built a newly introduced inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

It has been revealed that phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Sources indicate that phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

Recent findings suggest that A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a newly introduced one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

According to recent reports, we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

Sources indicate that one line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly demonstrates where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

Mr. Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

According to recent reports, stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. He also received the Federal CIO Council Leadership award for related work.

Recent findings suggest that prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

  • CISA has added two fresh vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added two newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Industry observers note that aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#1272. Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams

Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use.
  • Industry observers note that until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference.
  • Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information?

Industry observers note that until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.

Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review, trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform.

In a recent development, this post provides a condensed, actionable roadmap for the Platform team and Application teams building on agentic AI. It’s designed to be read together: the Platform team sets up the guardrails. Application teams build within them. Both need a shared language for where they are and what good looks like. We provide a Responsible AI Assessment Skill, that maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars to a three-phase maturity model: governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. For each phase, it indicates which responsible AI pillars are critical and when to revisit them. An accompanying scorecard lets both application teams and the platform team assess where they are today and iterate as their applications mature.

Note: This post covers the key questions to ask at each phase. It leaves out step-by-step implementation details. This post also doesn’t provide legal or compliance advice. Always consult your legal team.

In conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, four challenges surface consistently.

Figure 1: Agentic AI platforms introduce novel challenges regarding responsible AI.

According to recent reports, in this post, we define an agentic AI platform as described in AgentOps: Operationalize agentic AI at scale with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale, covering governance, build and operations, evaluation, and observability. Your responsible AI posture should mature progressively alongside this platform. We break the journey into three phases and present prioritized responsible AI pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline, allowing the platform team to establish a solid responsible AI foundation while their first use cases take shape.

In a recent development, figure 2: Overview of the proposed responsible AI maturity framework for agentic AI platforms. Teams integrate responsible AI over three phases.

Focus pillars: Governance, security and privacy.

Recent findings suggest that in this phase, assess project fit, risks, and ethics, secure legal and compliance approvals, and define the trust model for AI agents. The application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric. The Platform team focuses on establishing the core landing zone infrastructure, for example, setting up the overarching monitoring and access control, and governing newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start.

Critical tasks to consider in this phase include:.

Focus pillars: Safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, security and privacy.

Sources indicate that deploy your first agent that serves measurable business value. With the template and developer guidance provided from the Platform team, application teams implement orchestration patterns, memory, guardrail baselines, knowledge grounding, and tool use patterns. Risks identified in the foundation phase must now be addressed through a set of concrete controls in a pilot implementation.

In this phase, application teams consider the following concerns:.

Focus pillars: Fairness, explainability, transparency, security and privacy.

You have seen your first agent deliver business value. But how can you demonstrate it to a regulator, an auditor, or a board? How do you detect and help prevent unauthorized events on the system? In the third phase, evaluation stress-tests the fairness thresholds, and bias benchmarking. Hardening turns those findings into fixes.

This phase includes the following workstreams:.

According to recent reports, responsible AI isn’t a one-time implementation. As the platform evolves, each dimension must be periodically reassessed. The following table gives some examples to define both standing review cadences and event-driven triggers for re-evaluation.

According to recent reports, consider the following case: A bank builds a multi-agent loan processing platform. The platform features an intake agent, risk scoring agent, compliance agent, and customer communication agent.

In a recent development, phase 1 (Governance foundation): The platform team gathers legal requirements for their use case, for example those stemming from the EU AI Act and financial regulation, and registers agents at High-risk tier (financial decisions affecting individuals) using the AWS Agent Registry. They use a secure landing zone built with AWS Control Tower with foundational logging and access control active and configure tenant isolation to help prevent cross-customer leakage. The team documents residual risk and scope for each agent: for example, if the intake agent produces unexpected data, the risk scoring agent processes its output without independent verification.

Phase 2 (Pilot deployment: Validation and rollout): Risk scoring uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases grounded in regulatory lending documentation. Automated Reasoning checks verify denial decisions conform to documented criteria (conformance, not causal explanation). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redact PII data before customer communication. To address the multi-agent trust gap: the scoring agent confirms key applicant data from source systems rather than solely relying on the intake agent’s extraction. Each agent is bounded to required tools through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and the team uses Policies in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to further restrict the risk scoring agent to read-only access on the customer segment the agent is approved for. A case where the Automated Reasoning check returns a result other than VALID (for example, SATISFIABLE or TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS), or where the applicant’s risk score falls within the marginal band (for example, ±5 points of the threshold), is automatically escalated to a human credit specialist (human-in-the-loop review) before the decision is communicated. Escalation events are logged with the triggering condition for audit.

Phase 3 (Evaluation and hardening: Continuous monitoring): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, run on every pipeline push. CI/CD blocks deployment if an evaluation result is below releasing criterion or per-subgroup fairness metrics drifts beyond threshold. Red-team exercises (independent security team) test realistic security threats on the intake agent to verify that it can’t influence scoring. Human review of denial decisions, moving to after-the-fact review through an appeals process after 2,000 aligned decisions over 60 days. AI usage in the decision process is disclosed transparently to customers. Every automated decision is traced end-to-end using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It captures OpenTelemetry spans that can be automatically aggregated into a single distributed trace ready for auditing and appeals.

It has been revealed that frameworks serve as aspirations, while measurements provide accountability. Questions like “Can you list the risk tier for a use case?” will necessarily arise when the platform is operational from stakeholders like CISOs or auditors. To leave you prepared, we provide a repository with a set of questions that you can use to gauge your current posture and identify improvement areas before your system goes live.

In a recent development, we also package the questionnaire as a portable skill for AI Agents like Amazon Quick, and AI coding assistants like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex. The AI walks you through each phase and assesses your responsible AI posture along the dimensions on a scale from 1–5. Scores below 4 indicate substantial risks that should be remediated. Scores of 4 or higher indicate residual risk that might be acceptable when acknowledged on a case-by-case basis. The AI also provides actionable recommendations for improving your Responsible AI posture.

Figure 3: A portable AI skill that helps teams assess their Responsible AI posture through a set of questions.

Responsible AI (RAI) is a continuous, evolving effort. We recommend organizations implement RAI pillars through the AgentOps journey. These best practices cover governance policies, evaluation gates, and production telemetry into agentic AI platforms. This creates the feedback loop that keeps fairness, safety, and transparency continuously measured and improved.

This framework is a starting point, not an exhaustive compliance checklist. RAI practices vary by industry, use case, and requirements. Organizations should consult their own legal, compliance, and ethics teams to tailor these recommendations to their specific regulatory obligations and risk profiles.

For a comprehensive treatment of responsible AI across workload types, refer to the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, which provides detailed best practices, design principles, and evaluation criteria for each of the eight pillars discussed in this post. For industry-specific guidance, consult the Financial Services Industry Lens and the Healthcare Industry Lens, which address sector-specific regulatory and ethical requirements. Get started today by installing the RAI assessment skill from this repository and evaluating your organization’s RAI posture with your preferred AI agent.

Subnet Solutions reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. These vulnerabilities are not exploitable remotely. We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (fresh private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗.

It has been revealed that with these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:.

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Industry observers note that liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA has added one newly introduced vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-119977 WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#1263. How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1749 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro.
  • Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support?
  • LoanPro, the operating system for modern lenders, set out to change that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro.

Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? When a borrower calls a lender, the answering agent must pull account data from dozens of fields, transaction histories, and workflow queues to orient themselves before they can help the borrower. All the while, the clock runs. Assembling that context by hand means longer calls, inconsistent service quality, and agent frustration. A loan servicing assistant built on agentic AI changes that.

LoanPro, the operating system for modern lenders, set out to change that. Working with AWS Partner AllCloud and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro built a multi-agent AI assistant that gives servicing agents immediate access to synthesized borrower context and actionable next-step recommendations. Early results show customer call times reduced by up to 15 percent, according to AllCloud’s published case study.

Industry observers note that in this post, we walk through the business challenge, the agentic AI architecture built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the outcomes LoanPro achieved. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with the capabilities you need to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI.

Sources indicate that loanPro is a modern, API-first lending and credit platform that automates the entire loan lifecycle from origination to payoff. Founded in 2015, LoanPro serves as the system of record for lenders of every type: fintechs, banks and credit unions, and corporates that offer lending as a value-added service. According to LoanPro, the platform serves over 450 lenders, with loans managed on its platform reaching about 31 percent of US households. The platform powers loan management at enterprise scale across the financial services industry.

LoanPro isn’t a lender. It’s the operating system that lenders run on. That distinction matters because LoanPro’s AI strategy is designed to benefit the institutions it serves across the platform, not a single lending operation.

One of LoanPro’s core user groups is servicing agents: the people who manage borrower accounts, handle inbound calls, process payments, and resolve issues. During a live customer interaction, an agent might need to review:.

Recent findings suggest that before the AI assistant, agents navigated this information manually, moving through multiple screens and tabs to assemble the full picture. Less experienced agents took longer, and outcomes varied depending on who picked up the phone. LoanPro needed a solution that could:.

In a recent development, with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro partnered with AllCloud to design and build a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock. The assistant runs on Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock (see Models at a glance in Amazon Bedrock). Model availability varies by AWS Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models in Amazon Bedrock. It’s orchestrated with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Agent logic is built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source framework for building AI agents with tool use. The system coordinates specialized agents through a composer that routes each request to the right specialist, so each agent handles a focused task and can be evaluated and improved independently. The team chose these managed services over building the agent runtime and model access in-house. Amazon Bedrock provides access to leading foundation models through a single API, giving the team flexibility to adopt newly introduced models without managing separate endpoints. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed agent runtime that removes the operational overhead of running agents in production.

It has been revealed that figure 1 highlights this flow in implementation terms. A user request enters through LoanPro API v2 on Amazon API Gateway. An AWS Lambda handler places the request on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The Agent Interceptor Lambda function then invokes the Loan Summary Agent. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and uses Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. It reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The gateway finds the right tool in a catalog that the Loan Summary Service registers in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The Loan Summary Tool Lambda function validates the caller’s signature against LoanPro’s single sign-on (SSO) service. It then retrieves account data from LoanPro’s loan management system, which runs on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) behind a Network Load Balancer. The system’s role-based access controls validate the same signature. LoanPro also checks each request against the user’s permissions and compliance controls, then writes the action to its audit trail. The sections that follow describe these pieces: the multi-agent system, the tools it calls, and the gateway.

Figure 1: High-level architecture of the LoanPro AI servicing assistant.

The architecture has four key components, which combine the pieces in Figure 1 with the composer agent and Invoke API Tool that coordinate and act on them:.

The solution uses a multi-agent architecture built with the Strands Agents SDK. Rather than a single monolithic model handling every task, specialized agents collaborate to serve different parts of the servicing workflow. One agent focuses on data retrieval and account summarization. Another handles action selection and workflow recommendations. A composer agent routes each request to the right specialist and composes the final response. This separation of concerns makes each agent more straightforward to evaluate, tune, and extend independently.

Industry observers note that the agents retrieve borrower data from LoanPro’s internal systems through tool use, a capability in Amazon Bedrock for calling external functions and APIs. Two primary tools power the assistant:.

By connecting to LoanPro’s existing APIs, the assistant works with live production data without requiring a separate data pipeline or data warehouse.

AgentCore Gateway is the secure access layer between the agents and the tools they call. It exposes LoanPro’s APIs to the agents as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), handles authentication, and manages those connections. AWS Lambda, a serverless compute service that runs code without provisioning or managing servers, provides the integration layer between the gateway and LoanPro’s APIs. The team chose AgentCore Gateway with Lambda over a direct integration for three reasons. It centralizes authentication at a managed entry point, isolates LoanPro’s APIs behind a managed boundary, and lets new tools be added without redeploying the agents. This serverless approach keeps the infrastructure lightweight and scales automatically with request volume. In Figure 1, the Agent Interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime. AgentCore Gateway enforces this access control, screening each request before it reaches the Loan Summary Tool. Because the assistant operates in a regulated lending context, the production deployment pairs these components with additional controls. LoanPro’s role-based access controls and compliance guardrails apply to each request, and AI actions are written to LoanPro’s audit trail and attributed to a named, responsible person.

It has been revealed that the assistant is embedded directly into LoanPro’s existing web portal, the same interface servicing agents already use. Agents interact with the AI assistant through two components:.

LoanPro built the assistant with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, which pairs AWS applied scientists with customers and partners to accelerate generative AI initiatives, and AllCloud, an AWS Premier Consulting Partner. The three teams designed and built the solution together. What began as a focused engagement now runs in production, serving LoanPro’s servicing agents.

The work was organized into two parallel workstreams:.

The primary workstream built the AI assistant that is now running in production. Key activities included:.

In a recent development, loanPro had an existing proof of concept (POC) that used a large language model (LLM) to convert natural language into rule automation code for their Clojure rules engine. The core functionality worked, but the solution had known limitations: frequent timeouts, no monitoring, and no deployment strategy. AllCloud conducted architectural reviews and provided recommendations to bring this existing POC to a production-ready state, including a documented production architecture and risk assessment.

Sources indicate that A structured evaluation pipeline validated agent accuracy against benchmarks established by LoanPro’s subject-matter experts (SMEs). The team assembled a benchmark of 150 SME-labeled accounts. Against that benchmark, they measured the agent’s ability to retrieve data, summarize findings, and select appropriate actions, holding it to a 99 percent accuracy target that the agent met. This framework carries forward into production, giving LoanPro a repeatable process for measuring and improving agent performance over time.

Deploying the AI assistant delivered measurable operational impact:.

It has been revealed that “The AI assistant has changed how servicing agents work. Instead of spending the first few minutes of every call navigating screens and assembling context, agents now open an account and immediately see the full picture with prescriptive recommendations around the next actions to take. That time savings compounds across thousands of calls.”.

— Colin Terry, Chief Product Officer, LoanPro.

Building on the success of the servicing agent assistant, LoanPro and AllCloud are expanding their collaboration. The teams are developing additional AI agents to extend intelligent capabilities across more parts of the lending workflow, moving beyond servicing into areas such as collections and origination support.

The modular, multi-agent architecture makes this expansion practical. New agents can be built and deployed independently using the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore infrastructure, without redesigning the core system. As the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore continue to evolve, LoanPro prepares to incorporate new capabilities as they become available.

In this post, we indicated how LoanPro, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, and AllCloud built a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help servicing agents resolve borrower calls faster and more consistently. The solution retrieves data autonomously, generates account summaries in real time, and recommends next-best actions, reducing customer call times by up to 15 percent.

If you are building agentic AI solutions for customer-facing workflows, here are some resources to explore:.

To get started, explore the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building multi-agent systems, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for deploying agents at scale, or visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center to learn how AWS experts can help accelerate your own AI initiative.

#1256. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1949 w)
📖 Baca

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Sources indicate that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least key experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency problems which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Sources indicate that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least key experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Industry observers note that our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a recent development, in a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

Recent findings suggest that when we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

In a recent development, because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It highlights the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

It has been revealed that we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub problems autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

According to recent reports, notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments indicated that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

Sources indicate that HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

Industry observers note that the calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

According to recent reports, this command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

According to recent reports, to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

Recent findings suggest that HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S.
  • The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I]. Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F]. Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H]. Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O]. Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.
